sub: A reluctant prophet, a repentant city, and a very big fish. Study how this story is built — its genre, its ironies, its techniques — and prove every answer from the clues.

brief.label: Your mission
brief.h: Read the story, not the sermon
brief.p: You are a literary analyst studying how the Book of Jonah is constructed: its genre, its heavy use of irony, and what it reveals about the reluctant-messenger figure. Every answer must come from the clues.

win.h: You read Jonah like a literary critic!
win.p: You named the genre, spotted the reversals, identified the irony, and connected it to another reluctant hero — that is close literary reading.

clues.title: What kind of text is this?
clues.body: The Book of Jonah is a prophetic narrative — a story about a prophet, told with plot, character, and rising conflict. Unlike most prophetic books, it is almost entirely story rather than speeches.

clues.title: The prophet runs the wrong way
clues.body: God tells Jonah to go to Nineveh (east). Jonah boards a ship heading to Tarshish (west) — the opposite direction. A prophet who flees his own calling is the story's central irony.

clues.title: The 'villains' repent
clues.body: Nineveh is described as a great wicked city. Yet when Jonah finally delivers a five-word message, the entire city — king included — immediately repents. The supposed villains outperform the prophet.

clues.title: The prophet's reaction
clues.body: After the city repents and is spared, Jonah does not celebrate. He sits outside the city, angry that his doom prophecy did not come true. The text says he was 'exceedingly displeased.' The messenger resents his own message's success.

clues.title: Reluctant heroes in other stories
clues.body: Jonah belongs to the reluctant-messenger pattern found across literature. Katniss Everdeen in The Hunger Games resists becoming a symbol; Frodo in The Lord of the Rings reluctantly accepts a mission. All three are pushed into roles they try to avoid.

clues.title: True, but off topic
clues.body: The text says a 'great fish' swallowed Jonah for three days. Sperm whales, one real species large enough to swallow a human, can dive over 7,000 feet deep — a true marine-biology fact, but irrelevant to how the story uses irony.

locks.title: Name the genre
locks.q: Clue 1 names the genre of the Book of Jonah. What two-word genre label does it use? (Type both words.)
locks.reason: Clue 1 defines the Book of Jonah as a prophetic narrative — a story about a prophet built with plot, character, and conflict. Naming genre is the first move in literary analysis.

locks.title: Spot the irony
locks.q: The story's central irony, described in Clue 2, is that…
options: A prophet sails west instead of going east, running from the very mission he was given
A great fish can survive in the deep ocean for three days
Nineveh was the largest city in the ancient world
locks.reason: Clue 2 defines the central irony: Jonah is a prophet who runs the opposite direction from his assignment. Irony occurs when what happens is the reverse of what is expected.

locks.title: Find the real evidence of irony
locks.q: Check every item that names an actual ironic reversal in the story. Leave out the true-but-off-topic fact.

items.t: The 'wicked' city repents instantly while the prophet sulks
The prophet flees west when sent east — the opposite direction
Sperm whales can dive more than 7,000 feet deep
Jonah is angry that his own prophecy did not destroy the city

locks.reason: The whale-dive fact is true but has nothing to do with irony or literary craft. The three strong items each describe a reversal of expectation — the engine of irony in the text.

locks.title: Order the story's reversals
locks.q: Tap the three plot moments in the order the story presents them.
locks.reason: The narrative moves from flight (Clue 2) to the city's repentance (Clue 3) to Jonah's anger (Clue 4). Tracking sequence shows how each reversal builds on the last.

sub: A man is left on the road. Two expected helpers pass by. An outsider stops. Study how this parable is built — its genre, its reversals, and what it argues — and prove every answer from the clues.

brief.label: Your mission
brief.p: You are studying the Good Samaritan as literature: its genre, the reversal at its heart, and its 'show don't tell' technique. Every answer must come directly from the clues.

win.h: You read the parable like a literary analyst!
win.p: You named the genre, explained the reversal, caught the technique, and spotted the decoy — solid close reading.

clues.title: What kind of text is this?
clues.body: The Good Samaritan is a parable — a short fictional story used to make an ethical point. In the Gospel of Luke, Jesus tells it in response to the question 'Who is my neighbor?' The story is the argument.

clues.title: What happens on the road
clues.body: A man is beaten by robbers and left for dead on the road from Jerusalem to Jericho. Two figures — a priest and a Levite, both respected religious leaders in the story's culture — see him and pass by on the other side.

clues.title: The outsider becomes the hero
clues.body: A Samaritan — whom the original audience would have expected to be the least likely helper — stops, treats the wounded man's injuries, carries him to an inn, and pays for his care. The story's argument is made by reversing who the audience expected to act.

clues.title: A key technique
clues.body: The parable never states 'compassion matters' or 'outsiders can be good.' Instead it SHOWS the Samaritan bandaging wounds, pouring oil and wine, and paying the innkeeper. The moral is implied through action, not announced.

clues.title: The reversal in modern ethics
clues.body: The parable's pattern — the unexpected person does the right thing — appears in modern discussions of the bystander effect. Psychologists note that in a crowd, bystanders often pass by (like the priest and Levite), while one individual acts. The parable anticipates this ethical question.

clues.title: True, but off topic
clues.body: The Samaritan gives the innkeeper two denarii. A Roman denarius was a silver coin worth roughly one day's wage for a laborer in the ancient world — a true historical fact, but it does not explain how the parable makes its argument.

locks.title: Name the genre
locks.q: Clue 1 names this kind of short fictional story used to make an ethical point. What is the one-word genre?
locks.reason: Clue 1 defines a parable as a short fictional story used to make an ethical point. Identifying genre tells us how the text works and what it is trying to do.

locks.title: Order the events
locks.q: Tap the three story moments in the order the parable presents them.
locks.reason: The parable moves from the attack (Clue 2) to the two passersby (Clue 2) to the Samaritan's care and payment (Clue 3). Sequence is how the reversal builds its effect.

locks.title: Identify the technique
locks.q: Clue 4 describes a technique where the story shows the Samaritan bandaging wounds instead of stating 'compassion matters.' That technique is called…
locks.reason: Clue 4 defines 'show don't tell': the parable demonstrates the moral through action rather than announcing it. Naming this technique is a key move in literary analysis.

locks.title: Find the real literary evidence
locks.q: Check every item that names something that actually explains how the parable makes its argument. Leave out the true-but-off-topic fact.

items.t: The outsider (Samaritan) acts while expected helpers pass by — a reversal
The story shows bandaging and paying instead of stating a moral
A Roman denarius was worth about one day's wage
The parable is told as a response to the question 'Who is my neighbor?'

locks.reason: The denarius fact is true historical background but does not explain how the parable constructs its argument. The three strong items all show craft decisions that make the story work.

sub: The Psalms are poems — and poems are built with specific tools. Study the genre, the techniques of Hebrew poetry, and how they connect to poets you may already know.

brief.label: Your mission
brief.p: You are studying the Psalms as lyric poetry: their genre, their use of vivid imagery, and the Hebrew technique called parallelism. You will also connect these techniques to modern poems. Every answer must come from the clues.

win.h: You read the Psalms like a poet-critic!
win.p: You named lyric poetry, spotted parallelism and imagery, and connected ancient techniques to modern poets — that is literary analysis across time.

clues.title: What kind of text is this?
clues.body: The Psalms are lyric poetry — poems that express intense feeling, often using the first person ('I'). They were originally composed to be sung. The Book of Psalms contains 150 individual poems, each a separate literary work.

clues.title: Hebrew poetry's signature move
clues.body: Hebrew poets rarely used rhyme. Instead they used parallelism: stating an idea, then immediately restating or extending it in the next line. Psalm 23 opens: 'The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want.' Two lines, one idea, balanced — that is parallelism.

clues.title: Painting with words
clues.body: The Psalms build their emotional power through imagery — concrete pictures that make the reader see and feel. 'He makes me lie down in green pastures; he leads me beside still waters.' The calm is felt through the image, not stated.

clues.title: Parallelism in modern poetry
clues.body: Robert Frost's 'The Road Not Taken' uses balanced lines to weigh two choices. William Carlos Williams's 'This Is Just to Say' builds its feeling through pure imagery — cold plums, sweetness, the icebox — without explaining the emotion. Both techniques echo Hebrew poetry's playbook.

clues.title: What imagery does that a statement cannot
clues.body: Psalm 46 says: 'God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble. Therefore we will not fear, though the earth give way and the mountains fall into the heart of the sea.' The falling mountains are an image — they make abstract fear feel physical and real.

clues.title: True, but off topic
clues.body: Many Psalms include musical directions, and ancient Israelites used instruments including harps, lyres, and ram's-horn trumpets (shofars). The shofar is still used in Jewish worship today — a true fact, but it tells us nothing about how the Psalms use parallelism or imagery.

locks.title: Name the genre
locks.q: Clue 1 names the genre of the Psalms. What two-word label does it use for poems that express intense feeling, often in the first person?
locks.reason: Clue 1 defines the Psalms as lyric poetry — poems that express intense feeling in first person, originally sung. Genre identification frames how we read a text.

locks.title: Identify parallelism
locks.q: According to Clue 2, Hebrew poets used parallelism instead of rhyme. Which example best shows parallelism?
options: 'The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want' — the same idea restated in a balanced second line
Ram's-horn trumpets were used in ancient Israelite worship
The Book of Psalms contains exactly 150 poems
locks.reason: Clue 2 defines parallelism as stating an idea then restating or extending it in the next line — exactly what 'The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want' does. The other options are facts, not examples of the technique.

locks.title: Order the literary concepts
locks.q: Tap the three concepts in the order the clues introduce them.
locks.reason: Clue 1 introduces lyric poetry, Clue 2 introduces parallelism, and Clue 3 introduces vivid imagery. Tracking the order shows how the analyst builds a literary argument step by step.

locks.title: Find real literary evidence
locks.q: Check every item that names an actual technique or connection to how the Psalms work as poetry. Leave out the true-but-off-topic fact.

items.t: Parallelism restates or extends an idea in a balanced second line
Imagery makes abstract feelings physical — like mountains falling into the sea
Ancient Israelites used shofars (ram's-horn trumpets) in worship
Robert Frost and William Carlos Williams use techniques that echo Hebrew poetry

locks.reason: The shofar fact is true cultural history but tells us nothing about how the poetry is constructed. The three strong items each describe a technique or connection that explains how the Psalms work as literature.

sub: A queen hides her identity. A villain plots destruction. The audience knows what the characters do not. Study how the Book of Esther uses dramatic irony and reversal — as a work of narrative craft.

brief.label: Your mission
brief.p: You are studying the Book of Esther as a narrative: its genre, its use of dramatic irony (what the audience knows vs. what characters know), and its great reversal of fortune. Every answer must come from the clues.

win.h: You read Esther like a narrative analyst!
win.p: You named the genre, explained dramatic irony, traced the reversal, and spotted the decoy — that is literary analysis of narrative structure.

clues.title: What kind of text is this?
clues.body: The Book of Esther is a narrative — a story with characters, conflict, rising tension, and resolution. Literary scholars note it reads like a novella: a carefully plotted short work of prose fiction with suspense as a key effect.

clues.title: What the audience knows
clues.body: Esther is a Jewish woman who becomes queen of Persia, but she has not revealed her identity. The audience knows she is Jewish; her husband King Ahasuerus does not. This gap — audience knows, character does not — is dramatic irony.

clues.title: Haman's edict
clues.body: The king's official Haman hates Esther's cousin Mordecai and convinces the king to sign an edict ordering the destruction of all Jewish people in the kingdom. Haman builds a tall gallows specifically to hang Mordecai.

clues.title: Fortune flips completely
clues.body: When Esther reveals her identity and Haman's plot, the king reverses the situation entirely: Haman is hanged on the very gallows he built for Mordecai. The planned destruction becomes the destroyer's destruction — a complete reversal of fortune.

clues.title: Dramatic irony in other stories
clues.body: Dramatic irony is a technique across literature and film. In Romeo and Juliet, the audience knows Juliet is not dead while Romeo does not — with tragic results. In Esther, the irony creates suspense: we wait for the moment the king finally learns what we already know.

clues.title: True, but off topic
clues.body: The Persian Empire under Ahasuerus (also known as Xerxes I) was one of the largest empires in history, stretching from India to Ethiopia across 127 provinces. This is historically documented — but the empire's size does not explain how the Book of Esther uses dramatic irony.

locks.title: Name the technique
locks.q: Clue 2 describes a technique where the audience knows Esther is Jewish but the king does not. What is this technique called? (Two words.)
locks.reason: Clue 2 defines dramatic irony as the gap between what the audience knows and what a character knows. Naming this technique is the first move in analyzing how the narrative creates suspense.

locks.title: Identify the reversal
locks.q: The great reversal of fortune in the story, described in Clue 4, is best described as…
options: Haman is hanged on the gallows he built for Mordecai, turning his plan against him
The Persian Empire stretched from India to Ethiopia across 127 provinces
Esther becomes queen by hiding her Jewish identity from the king
locks.reason: Clue 4 describes the reversal: Haman's planned destruction is turned completely against him. Reversal of fortune is a specific narrative technique where a character's plan produces the opposite result.

locks.title: Order the plot events
locks.q: Tap the three plot moments in the order the narrative presents them.

pads.e: 🔄 Haman hanged on his own gallows

locks.reason: The narrative moves from Esther's hidden identity (Clue 2) to Haman's edict (Clue 3) to the final reversal (Clue 4). Ordering events shows how the reversal is set up and paid off.

locks.title: Find real narrative evidence
locks.q: Check every item that names an actual technique or plot element that shows how the story is built. Leave out the true-but-off-topic fact.

items.t: The audience knows Esther is Jewish while the king does not — dramatic irony
The Persian Empire stretched from India to Ethiopia across 127 provinces
Haman's gallows becomes the instrument of his own destruction — reversal
The story reads like a novella with rising tension and suspense

locks.reason: The empire-size fact is true historical background but does not explain how the narrative is constructed. The three strong items each describe a craft technique — genre, irony, reversal — that shows how the story works.

sub: Two women claim the same baby. A king proposes a shocking test. Study how this scene is built as an argument — a logic puzzle designed to force the truth to reveal itself.

brief.label: Your mission
brief.h: Read the test as an argument
brief.p: You are analyzing Solomon's judgment (1 Kings) as rhetoric and logic: how a cleverly designed test forces the truth to emerge. Every answer must come from the clues — no outside knowledge needed.

win.h: You read Solomon's judgment like a rhetorician!
win.p: You named the genre, explained the logic of the test, identified the rhetorical technique, and spotted the decoy — that is analytical reading.

clues.title: What kind of text is this?
clues.body: This passage from 1 Kings is a narrative — a short story — but it is structured as a logical argument. The scene presents a problem (two women, one claim), a test (Solomon's proposal), and a proof (one woman's reaction reveals the truth). It reads like a logic puzzle embedded in a story.

clues.title: An unresolvable dispute
clues.body: Two women both claim to be the mother of a living baby. There are no witnesses. King Solomon cannot know who is telling the truth from testimony alone — both women say the same thing. The dispute seems impossible to resolve.

clues.title: Solomon's proposal
clues.body: Solomon orders a sword to be brought and proposes to cut the baby in two, giving half to each woman. The proposal is extreme on purpose — it is designed not to be carried out, but to force a reaction that reveals who is telling the truth.

clues.title: Why the test works
clues.body: The real mother immediately surrenders her claim, saying 'Give her the child — do not kill it.' The other woman agrees to the division. Solomon's logic: only the true mother would rather lose the child than see it harmed. The emotional reaction becomes the evidence.

clues.title: Forcing truth through a test
clues.body: The structure of Solomon's judgment — design a situation where only the truth-teller would respond a certain way — appears in logic and law. In literature, Sherlock Holmes repeatedly uses this technique: arrange a scenario and observe who reacts in the revealing way.

clues.title: True, but off topic
clues.body: According to 1 Kings, Solomon's throne was made of ivory and overlaid with gold, with six steps and twelve lion statues flanking each side — an elaborate description of royal wealth. This is in the text, but it tells us nothing about how Solomon's logical test is constructed.

locks.title: Explain the logic
locks.q: According to Clue 4, Solomon's test works because…
options: Only the true mother would rather lose the child than see it harmed, so her reaction is the evidence
The king had two witnesses who identified the real mother
The ivory-and-gold throne gave Solomon divine authority to judge
locks.reason: Clue 4 explains the logic: the real mother's reaction — surrendering her claim to save the child — is itself the proof. The test is designed so that only the truth-teller would respond that way.

locks.title: Name the genre blend
locks.q: Clue 1 says this passage is a narrative structured as something else — a type of reasoning puzzle. What two-word phrase does it use?
locks.reason: Clue 1 describes the passage as a 'logic puzzle embedded in a story' — a narrative that works like a logical argument. Identifying this blend explains why the scene reads the way it does.

locks.title: Order the argument's steps
locks.q: Tap the three moves in Solomon's argument in the order they happen.
locks.reason: The argument moves from the unsolvable problem (Clue 2) to Solomon's designed test (Clue 3) to the reaction that proves the truth (Clue 4). Sequencing these steps shows how the argument is logically structured.

locks.title: Find the real analytical evidence
locks.q: Check every item that explains how Solomon's test works as logic or rhetoric. Leave out the true-but-off-topic fact.

items.t: The test is designed to produce a reaction only the truth-teller would have
Solomon's throne was made of ivory and gold with twelve lion statues
The dispute was impossible to resolve from testimony alone — no witnesses
The mother's emotional response becomes the evidence in the argument

locks.reason: The throne description is a true detail from 1 Kings but has nothing to do with how the logical test is constructed. The three strong items each explain a step in the argument's design.
